name: Arches National Park
blurb: Soil crust, kangaroo rats and cougars in Utah's red-rock desert.

tip.title: Dry out the desert
tip.text: Rain is scarce already. Set Rain & snowmelt to -100% and watch the crust and shrubs, then the deer, rabbits and rodents that depend on them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Biological soil crust
nodes.desc: A living skin of cyanobacteria, lichens, mosses, algae and microfungi. It binds sand grains against erosion, soaks up scarce rain and fixes nitrogen, but is easily broken by footsteps.

nodes.name: Indian ricegrass
nodes.desc: A tufted desert grass of sandy soils that is listed among the common plants of Arches. Its seeds are food for desert rodents.

nodes.name: Blackbrush
nodes.desc: A dense, dark shrub that is among the most recorded plants of the park and a common cover on its higher, drier ground.

nodes.name: Prickly pear
nodes.desc: A spiny cactus, one of the park's most frequently recorded plants. Its pads store water in a land that gets under 10 inches of rain a year.

nodes.name: Utah juniper
nodes.desc: A drought-tough tree of dry slopes. Its berry-like cones feed birds and small mammals, and jackrabbits and rodents help spread its seeds.

nodes.name: Mule deer
nodes.desc: The park's most recorded large mammal. It mostly browses shrubs and trees, adds forbs in summer, and is a main prey of cougars.

nodes.name: Desert bighorn sheep
nodes.desc: A sure-footed grazer of rocky canyon country, listed among Arches' wildlife. Cougars prey on bighorn sheep.

nodes.name: Black-tailed jackrabbit
nodes.desc: A big-eared hare of open desert shrubland that eats plants and carries juniper seeds. It is prey for snakes, bobcats and other predators.

nodes.name: Desert cottontail
nodes.desc: A small rabbit that is active at dawn and dusk and eats plants. Rattlesnakes, bullsnakes and bobcats take it.

nodes.name: Ord's kangaroo rat
nodes.desc: A nocturnal seed-eater that stores seeds in burrows and gets most of its water from its food. Coyotes, bobcats, owls and snakes eat it.

nodes.name: White-tailed antelope squirrel
nodes.desc: A day-active omnivore that eats mostly plants and seeds, plus arthropods. Raptors, canids and snakes prey on it.

nodes.name: Common raven
nodes.desc: By far the most recorded species near Arches. An opportunistic omnivore and scavenger that will eat carrion and take snakes and small birds.

nodes.name: Turkey vulture
nodes.desc: A soaring scavenger that feeds on carrion, from small rodents to deer, helping recycle dead animals back into the web.

nodes.name: Bullsnake
nodes.desc: A large day-active constrictor that eats rodents, rabbits, lizards and birds. It is itself prey for ravens and bobcats.

nodes.name: Western rattlesnake
nodes.desc: A pit viper of rocky ground (the Arches form is the Grand Canyon rattlesnake). It eats small mammals such as cottontails and lizards.

nodes.name: Cougar
nodes.desc: A nocturnal big cat that lives in desert and mountains and prefers large prey such as mule deer and bighorn sheep.

nodes.name: Bobcat
nodes.desc: A nocturnal small cat that hunts rabbits, rodents, birds and snakes, and takes mostly fawns or weak animals among deer.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Strong desert sun drives plant growth and bakes the bare rock and sand, so plants only thrive where water is also available.

nodes.name: Rain & snowmelt
nodes.desc: Under 10 inches of rain fall a year, and unpredictably. The soil crust absorbs and holds what does arrive.

nodes.name: Sandy desert soil
nodes.desc: Thin, easily eroded soils of the Colorado Plateau. Nitrogen and nutrients are scarce and the crust helps hold the soil in place.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi, bacteria and insects break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil.
